title: Escape the Hacker
intro: Complete all five missions at your own pace to escape the hacker, then build your final challenge poster.

blocks.html:
🚨 Mission Briefing

A hacker has broken into the school network. Only you can stop them. Complete five missions to escape, then take on the final challenge.

Learning objective: to explain how hackers steal information, and to describe how phishing, strong passwords and encryption keep us safe.

How this lesson works: work through the missions in order, at your own speed. Headphones on before Mission 1. Your work saves by itself as you go — watch for the green Saved label at the top of the page.

  • 🎥 Mission 1 — How hackers steal information
  • 🎣 Mission 2 — Spot the phishing emails
  • 🔐 Mission 3 — Password strength challenge
  • 🔎 Mission 4 — Caesar cipher puzzle
  • 🧠 Mission 5 — Cybersecurity quiz
  • 🏆 Final challenge — Design a poster

blocks.title: 🎥 Mission 1 — How hackers steal information
blocks.note: Headphones on. Watch the whole video. You can pause and rewatch as many times as you need — then answer the question underneath.

blocks.prompt: 🎥 Mission 1 debrief. Name two different ways a hacker can steal someone's information, and say which of the two you think is easiest for a hacker to do.
blocks.criteria: A good answer names two distinct methods (such as phishing, guessing or cracking passwords, malware, fake websites, public wi-fi snooping, or shoulder surfing) and gives a reason for the one chosen as easiest.

blocks.title: 🎣 Mission 2 — Spot the phishing emails
blocks.note: A phishing email pretends to be someone you trust so you hand over your details. Read each email carefully. Look at who really sent it, how it makes you feel, and what it wants you to click. Choose an answer for each, then press Check my answers.

questions.q:
From: Netflix-Support <billing@netfIix-account.co>
Subject: URGENT!! Your account will be DELETED in 24 hours

"Dear Customer, we could not take your payment. Click here NOW to enter your card details or you will lose all your shows forever."
options: Phishing — it is a scam
Safe — a normal email from Netflix
questions.why: Spot on. Look at the sender address — it is spelled with a capital I instead of an L. It also rushes you with a scary deadline and asks for card details. Real companies never do this.
questions.hint: Read the sender's address very carefully, letter by letter. Then ask yourself: why is it in such a hurry?

questions.q:
From: Mrs Chowdhury <a.chowdhury@yourschool.sch.uk>
Subject: Homework due Friday

"Hi Year 9, the worksheet we started in class is on the school system under Week 4. See me at lunch if you are stuck."
options: Phishing — it is a scam
Safe — a normal email from a teacher
questions.why: Correct. The address is the real school domain, it does not rush you, it asks for nothing personal, and it points to somewhere you already have access to.
questions.hint: Does this email ask you for any personal details, passwords or money? Does it try to panic you?

questions.q:
From: Free Gaming Prizes <winner@freeprize-vbucks.ru>
Subject: You have won 10,000 V-Bucks!!!

"Congratulations!!! You are our 1,000,000th visitor. Just log in with your Epic Games username and password to claim your prize."
options: Phishing — it is a scam
Safe — a real competition win
questions.why: Exactly. You cannot win a competition you never entered, and no real company ever asks you to type your password into an email to claim a prize.
questions.hint: Did you ever enter this competition? And what exactly is it asking you to hand over?

questions.q:
From: IT Helpdesk <it.support@yourschool.sch.uk>
Subject: Password reset

"Your password expires today. Reply to this email with your current username and password so we can reset it for you."
options: Phishing — it is a scam
Safe — the school IT team need it
questions.why: Well spotted — this one is tricky because the address looks right. But real IT staff never need your password, and no one should ever send a password in an email. Senders' addresses can be faked.
questions.hint: The address looks genuine, so ignore it for a moment. Would a real IT technician ever need to be told your password?

blocks.title: 🔐 Mission 3 — Password strength challenge
blocks.task: Your challenge: invent a password that ticks all five boxes below. Type it into the box and watch the bar. Then try these and see what happens: 'password1', your favourite football team, and three random words joined together with numbers and symbols. Which one is strongest? When all five ticks are green, you have beaten the mission — then answer the question underneath.

blocks.prompt: 🔐 Mission 3 debrief. Why is a long password made of several random words safer than a short one with a few symbols in it? And why should you never use the same password for two different accounts?
blocks.criteria: A good answer says that length means many more possible combinations so it takes a computer far longer to guess, and that reusing a password means one leaked account lets an attacker into all the others.

blocks.title: 🔎 Mission 4 — Caesar cipher puzzle
blocks.task: The hacker left a coded message behind. They used a Caesar cipher: every letter was moved along the alphabet by the same secret number of places. Drag the shift slider one step at a time and watch the green text underneath. When it turns into real English words, you have cracked it — type the message into the box and check it.
blocks.prompt: Type the hidden message here (letters only, spaces are fine):

blocks.title: 🧠 Mission 5 — Cybersecurity quiz
blocks.note: Five questions to prove you are ready to escape. Choose an answer for each one, then press Check my answers. If you get one wrong, read the hint and try again.

options: Tricking someone into giving away their private details
A virus that deletes all your files
Guessing a password by trying every combination
Watching what someone types on public wi-fi
questions.why: Yes — phishing is a trick that fools a person, not a machine. That is why being careful matters as much as any software.
questions.hint: Think back to Mission 2. Were those emails attacking the computer, or attacking the person reading them?

questions.q: Which of these is the strongest password?
options: Chelsea2011
P@ssw0rd
correct-horse-battery-42!
MyName123
questions.why: Correct. It is long, mixes letter types, uses a symbol and a number, and is not based on anything a hacker could look up about you.
questions.hint: Length beats cleverness. Which one is the longest, and which ones contain something a stranger could find out about you?

questions.q: A Caesar cipher keeps a message secret by…
options: Deleting some of the letters
Moving every letter along the alphabet by the same amount
Turning the letters into numbers at random
Hiding the message inside a picture
questions.why: That is it — and because the shift is always the same, someone who works out the shift can read the whole message. That is why modern encryption is far more complicated.
questions.hint: Think about what you did with the slider in Mission 4. What was it changing?

questions.q: An email says you must click a link within one hour or lose your account. What should you do?
options: Click the link quickly before time runs out
Reply asking if it is real
Do not click. Go to the website yourself, or tell an adult
Forward it to your friends to warn them
questions.why: Exactly right. Making you panic is the whole trick. Going to the real website yourself means you never touch the hacker's link.
questions.hint: A scammer wants you to act fast and stop thinking. What is the calmest, safest thing you could do instead?

questions.q: Why does two-factor authentication (getting a code on your phone) make an account safer?
options: It makes your password longer
A hacker needs your password AND your phone to get in
It hides your password from the website
It stops the website from being hacked
questions.why: Perfect. Even if a hacker steals your password, they are stopped at the second door because they do not have your phone.
questions.hint: 'Two-factor' means two separate things are needed. If a hacker had only one of them, could they still get in?

blocks.html:
🏆 Final challenge — Escape the hacker

You have beaten all five missions. To escape for good, teach everybody else how to stay safe.

Your task: design a cybersecurity poster for students in Year 7. Use paper, Canva or PowerPoint.

Your poster must include all five of these:

  • A title that grabs attention
  • Two warning signs of a phishing email (use Mission 2 to help you)
  • Three rules for making a strong password (use Mission 3)
  • One sentence explaining what encryption does (use Mission 4)
  • Something a Year 7 should do if they think they have been hacked

Make it clear, not crowded. Big text, short sentences, and a picture or icon for each rule. Imagine it on the wall of the computing room — could someone understand it from two metres away?

Stuck for a title? Try starting with a question, like "Would you spot a fake email?"

blocks.prompt: 🏁 Paste the link to your finished poster
blocks.note: Save your poster as a PDF, or photograph your paper design. Upload it to your OneDrive, choose Share, copy the link, and paste it above. Your work saves automatically. If you cannot get the link to work, tell your teacher — do not lose your poster!
